- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.1) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% to avoid missing downward momentum.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >5% from prior period), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a 2–5% downward correction to prevent overreaction.
- If model shows strong mean reversion bias (e.g., forecasting back to historical mean after volatility), check sentiment for reversal signals — if sentiment is neutral or turning, reduce mean-reversion strength.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often underestimates near the end of the horizon when sentiment is weak; add 0.5–1.5% to final forecast if sentiment <0.2.
- If sentiment is high and model forecast is low, consider a “sentiment-adjusted” upward bias — add 0.5–1.5% to forecast if sentiment >0.4 and price is below 60.
- Avoid forecasting below 55% of recent 18-day average unless sentiment is strongly negative — use sentiment as a trigger for floor correction.
